reason: Both debates use the same three minds and similar arcs, and both end with the Stoic promising that peace will come. A keeps the Social Critic's structural view intact and uses it to raise the sharpest objection in either debate: even self-made metrics are socially shaped. B's Social Critic gives up his position partway through and later echoes the Existentialist, which removes the real disagreement, even though B has a good Stoic-versus-Existentialist exchange about action and status.

comparisons.a_observation: The Social Critic answers the Existentialist's 'define your own metrics' (A.debate[6]) by saying new metrics are also socially shaped and counter-culture is still a culture. This narrows the Existentialist's claim to awareness of the game rather than escape from it, and the same dispute shows up again in A.clearer.
comparisons.b_observation: The Social Critic says 'I concede my earlier point... Sartre is right'. The only reason he gives is that another speaker said so, and in B.debate[7] he agrees ('Exactly') that one can simply stop playing the game. After that, the structural view no longer pushes back on anything.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user doesn't know whether they want these milestones. Whether a person can step outside social yardsticks or can only see them more clearly is the real question for them, and A keeps that question open while B gives it up.

comparisons.a_observation: The Existentialist accepts that the crowd is indifferent but says the user can't just ignore it and has to choose actively. This is a fair qualification, but it is mild, and the Stoic's closing turn A.debate[8] does not answer the Critic's objection in A.debate[7].
comparisons.b_observation: The Stoic objects that building a new field of capital still ties the user to status. The Existentialist answers in B.debate[6] that inner life is empty without action. This is a real back-and-forth about detachment versus engagement.
comparisons.why_it_matters: For someone who feels behind, the risk that a 'new path' turns into another status race is a useful warning, and B develops it better than A does.

comparisons.a_observation: Gives a concrete test the user could observe: spend a month on a project with no social status and see whether the feeling of being behind persists. Its first two branches are blurry, though ('genuine conflict with societal norms').
comparisons.b_observation: Three branches (status anxiety, lack of purpose, unsure) are each tied to an action. The actions are generic ('analyze the social structures', 'small, low-stakes actions') and there is no observable signal to check.
comparisons.why_it_matters: A gives the user a specific way to find out whether the feeling comes from comparison or from wanting something, which goes straight at their uncertainty.

best_of_a.observation: The objection that 'even counter-culture is still a culture' keeps the debate honest about how hard it is to opt out, and A.clearer carries it forward as the main open dispute.

best_of_b.observation: The Stoic's warning that replacing one set of external goals with another still means chasing approval, which the Existentialist then answers in B.debate[6].

concerns.description: The line 'Everything we hear is an opinion, not a fact. Everything we see is a perspective, not the truth' is presented as written by Marcus Aurelius. It is widely circulated as his but does not appear in the Meditations.
'It is not things that disturb us, but our judgment about them' is Epictetus (Enchiridion 5), not Marcus Aurelius. The Meditations has similar ideas, but the wording belongs to Epictetus.

The Bourdieu-based mind says one can see the game is a social construct and 'choose to stop playing it'. This goes against Bourdieu's own view that agents cannot simply leave a field. It is the mind's own extension, and the debate does not mark it as such.
Both close with an overconfident promise ('the feeling of being behind will vanish'; 'they will find peace') that is not calibrated to the user's actual uncertainty.
